fixes.explanation: That's the one, friend. The Teacher says a man's wisdom brightens his face, and the sternness of his face is changed. Wisdom works like a warm oven on a cold morning, because it warms up the whole look of a person. Wise folks tend to look like they just remembered where they left the good cookies.

No face gets covered in this verse. The Teacher says a man's wisdom brightens his face. Wisdom turns the lights on, it doesn't pull the curtains shut. He even says the sternness of his face is changed.

Right on the money. The Teacher says, “Keep the king’s command, I say, because of your oath before God.” So this is about a promise made before God. A promise like that is worth keeping, friend, even when keeping it is a pain.

The verse says it the other way around. The Teacher says the king's word is supreme, and then asks who can say to him, what are you doing. It's a question with no one named to answer it. So this one is false, friend.

Hold on, friend, the Teacher says it flat out: “Whoever keeps his command will come to no harm…” That's right there in the verse, so true is the answer, not false. I know a promise that big sounds almost too good, like a cookie that came out perfect on the first try. Go ahead and squint at it again, because it's still sitting there.

Plenty of us wish we could steer a neighbor's thoughts, friend, but the Teacher never goes there. His two things are the wind, which no man has power over to contain, and the day of death, which no one has authority over. Neighbors don't make the list.

The verse says the reverse. The Teacher says no one can be discharged in wartime, and so wickedness will not release those who practice it. That's the opposite of letting them leave any time they like. So this one is false, friend.

Right, false. The Teacher says that as no one can be discharged in wartime, “…so wickedness will not release those who practice it.” The card says they can leave any time they like, but the verse says wickedness won't release them. It's a hard line, so I won't joke on it.

That's the one, friend. The Teacher says the wicked who used to go in and out of the holy place “…were praised in the city where they had done so.” Then he says, “This too is futile.” I think that scene bothered him.
You'd expect that, and so would I. But the Teacher says they were praised in the city where they had done so. Then he says, “This too is futile.” I bet a curse is what most of us would have guessed.
A banishment would at least feel fair. But the Teacher reports their burial and says they were praised in the city where they had done so. Then he writes, “This too is futile.”

You'd think slow justice would keep folks nervous, but the verse goes somewhere else. The Teacher says hearts “…become fully set on doing evil.” Fear of the judge isn't mentioned. That's a hard thing to read.

Nice try, friend, but that word isn't in this verse. The Teacher says it will go well with those who fear God, who are reverent in His presence. The blank wants fear. That's the group he's pointing to.

Wouldn't that be nice? But the Teacher sees something harder. He says there are righteous men who get what the actions of the wicked deserve, and then he says, “I say that this too is futile.” I bet a double reward would have made a happier verse.

True, friend. The Teacher says, “…and there are wicked men who get what the actions of the righteous deserve.” It's the same verse flipped around, like somebody swapped the labels on the cookie boxes. Some righteous men get what the wicked deserve, and some wicked men get what the righteous deserve. He says plainly that this too is futile.

I get why you'd hesitate, but the verse says it plainly, so this one is true. The Teacher says there are wicked men who get what the actions of the righteous deserve. That's the second half of what he sees in this verse, right after the righteous men who get what the wicked deserve. He calls the whole thing futile.

Teaching it would be great, but that isn't what the Teacher says. He says a man is unable to comprehend the work that is done under the sun. Even if the wise man claims to know, he says, he is unable to comprehend.
